query_title: Add a pull with rebase action to the git viewlet
original_title: Feature request: more complete git integration
[php] highlighting  for mysql in php file
query_body:
Language injections is a feature of IDEs like Webstorm and PHPStorm that auto-detects when a language is use inside another language and then shows syntax highlighting for that _injected_ language. VS Code currently supports this in a few places:
- [INLINE_CODE] tags in HTML get CSS highlighting and IntelliSense
- [INLINE_CODE] tags in HTML get JS highlighting and IntelliSense
- HTML in a PHP file outside of [INLINE_CODE] gets highlighting but no IntelliSense

But there are many other contexts where this would be helpful, that are currently not supported and impossible to all hardcode:
- [INLINE_CODE] attribute in HTML contain CSS
- String literals in languages like PHP often contain SQL, see #1361. PHPStorm supports this for PHP, but Webstorm for example does not support this for NodeJS. It should really be supported in any language.
- String literals commonly contain HTML in Javascript or PHP (e.g. with jQuery, Angular or Vue templates)
- String literals commonly contain GraphQL queries in JavaScript
- HTML event attributes contain Javascript, like [INLINE_CODE]
- Countless HTML attributes in the Angular framework have Javascript-like expressions in them, like [INLINE_CODE], but also the mustache syntax [INLINE_CODE].
- [INLINE_CODE] contain Angular templates which is nothing but HTML. This pattern of templates in script tags exists in many of the major client side MVC frameworks.
- Javascript has RegExp literals. In other languages like PHP, RegExps are passed as strings. This is also the case in tasks.json problem matchers for VS Code (RegExp inside JSON string)

All of these examples currently don't get colored and receive no autocompletion. It would be awesome if VS Code was able to automatically detect languages in any context (like string literals, HTML attributes and tags) by some language patterns, like [INLINE_CODE] tags for HTML/XML, keywords like [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], etc. for SQL or template string tags like [INLINE_CODE] for GraphQL. This could be contributed by extensions or language servers.

This would be one of the best features VS Code could offer.

query_title: Provide support to synchronize settings across machines
original_title: [ExtensionDev] Expose API to get at file system locations
query_body:
There are quiet some extensions out there to handle setting synchronization between multiple computers. And in my opinion they are very important: Since vscode is very customizable with settings, keyboardshortcuts and extension it is very hard to synchronize those things between multiple workstations. And all those extensions are not really clean solutions, because vscode does nearly nothing to support them (for example the paths vscode uses are not exposed, see #2741).

So here some ideas to make synchronization clean and extensible:
- add a contribution point for synchronization extensions
 - Those extensions should not have to gather all the files that have to be synced. vscode should do this and then pass them to the extensions
 - Such an extension's job is only to upload/download the files, passed to them (so we can have the [INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE]/[INLINE_CODE].
 - Or maybe gather all settings into one big json object and pass that.
 - Support versioning and non versioning extensions
- add a remote_settings.json to build on top of the workspace-settings/user-settings stack.
- allow automatic and user triggered synchronization

Ok... just some ideas :smile:

query_title: VSCode should flag errors on tsconfig.json
query_body:
VS Code does not report errors in [INLINE_CODE], and then silently drops the ball without telling the user. This is particularly annoying since some things might continue working, while others mysteriously stop.

Errors in [INLINE_CODE] come in two flavours – actual syntactical errors, but also unrecognized new properties. In particular the latter is annoying, for example when TypeScript adds new features such as [INLINE_CODE] (see #3428).

My suggestion would be to at least visibly and loudly report this, but preferably be more lenient about what's accepted (e.g. unrecognized properties).

query_title: Better handle first-time opening of workspaces with explicit typescript.tsdk specified
original_title: typescript.tsdk doesn't work as workspace setting
query_body:
See #26046 for context.

The reason why VS Code does not implicitly use the workspace TS version is claimed to be for security reasons: if you clone a repo that has a malicious TS version in its [INLINE_CODE], the current behaviour prevents that code from being run implicitly.

This is a nonsensical argument because it assumes that nothing should be done implicitly when the user performs an explicit action - if we follow said argument to its conclusion, then nothing should happen when you open a VS Code workspace, or when you press the power button on your computer. **An explicit user action always has implicit elements.**

A more convincing argument is likely "Microsoft doesn't want to get sued/have its name in the news because an idiot cloned a malicious repo and it stole all his bitcoins" or "we don't want script kiddies making a plethora of repos with hacked TS versions in them to try and catfish unwary devs".

Regardless, the current behaviour of having to explicitly select the workspace TS version the first time you open a workspace is both irritating and barely a step above just implicitly using that version. After all, there is no "hey this could pwn your machine are you sure?" prompt when you actually select the workspace version.

A global setting "preferWorkspaceTypeScriptVersion" would essentially cover this scenario. By default it's [INLINE_CODE] which means do the current behaviour. If a user sets it to [INLINE_CODE] (implicit action, therefore safe!) then the workspace TS version is always used.

If that's not suitable (because a user could copy someone else's global VS Code config with "preferWorkspaceTypeScriptVersion" = [INLINE_CODE] and then they would not explicitly assent to running the TS code they downloaded, oh the humanity!) then the least-effort best-experience way of making this better is to simply add a Yes/No dialog that pops up the first time opening a workspace with [INLINE_CODE] specified, that asks the user if they want to use the workspace TS version (with appropriate "you could get pwned and Microsoft won't be held responsible" warnings), or the VS Code builtin version.

query_title: Open URL links with custom protocol schema
original_title: VS Code doesn't open links with custom URL schema
query_body:
Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes

- VS Code Version: 1.74.2 (but reasonable to assume it affects all previous versions as well)
- OS Version: macOS 10.14 (may not be dependent on OS version)

Steps to Reproduce:

1. Grab a file that offers clicking on links. It can be a [INLINE_CODE] tag in a PHP PHPDoc tag, an [CODE_BLOCK] in MD file (where [INLINE_CODE] is the actual url) or any similar.
2. Create a link using a protocol other than [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE] or [INLINE_CODE], that is registered in the OS. A good example can be the fairly common [INLINE_CODE], but there are many to try, such as [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE] etc. See a list of well known protocols [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_URI_schemes).

Expected behaviour:
The clicked link should be opened by using the applications registered in the OS to handle the given protocol. Browsers usually do it perfectly for any protocol.

Actual behaviour:
VSCode ignores the protocol and tries to resolve the path as a file, which may succeed in some cases, but fails most the time. But even when succeeds, it results in the file being opened in VSCode editor instead of the associated URL handler program registered in the OS.

Ideal behaviour would be:
Anything matched by [INLINE_CODE] (or maybe a bit more sophisticated matching respecting [RFC 3986](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt) completely) should be clickable, regardless of protocol, and the protocol handling should be handed over to the OS if VSCode does not understand it.



The same issue has been closed without resolution before. See #104429.
